name: Kojiki
info: The Kojiki is an early Japanese chronicle of myths, genealogies and semi-historical accounts of the kami and the imperial line, which its preface says Ō no Yasumaro compiled for Empress Genmei in 711–712.

facts.made: Ō no Yasumaro, a courtier, who according to the preface wrote down at Empress Genmei's order what the court attendant Hieda no Are had memorised at Emperor Tenmu's command
facts.form: A chronicle in three volumes, written mostly in Classical Chinese, with dozens of short songs and poems in Old Japanese transcribed phonetically in man'yōgana
facts.where: Known from late manuscripts, the oldest the Shinpukuji-bon of 1371–1372, and from printed editions and translations
facts.known: The creation of the islands by Izanagi and Izanami; Amaterasu hiding in the Heavenly Rock Cave; Susanoo and the serpent Yamata-no-Orochi; Ōkuninushi; the descent of Ninigi; Emperor Jimmu's conquest of Yamato; the oldest extant literary work in Japan

t: The Kojiki gathers myths, genealogies, songs and early imperial history into one account that presents the Yamato line as descended from heavenly deities and as rightful heir to the land.
Its preface says it was written down by Ō no Yasumaro from what Hieda no Are had memorised, and it is usually considered the oldest extant literary work in Japan.
Neglected in the Heian and Kamakura periods, it was raised to the status of a sacred text by the nativist scholars of the Edo period and, above all, by Motoori Norinaga's Kojiki-den.
dyk: Motoori Norinaga spent 34 years, from 1764 to 1798, on his 44-volume study of the Kojiki, the Kojiki-den. He valued the Kojiki over the Nihon Shoki because it was free of what he called Chinese mentality.
ev: Prince Shotoku and Soga no Umako undertake the first concerted effort at historical compilation of which a record survives
The Isshi incident burns Soga no Emishi's estate, and of the court's early records only the Kokki survives the fire
Ō no Yasumaro presents the Kojiki to Empress Genmei, having been ordered to compile it in 711
The Shinpukuji-bon manuscript, the oldest existing copy, is made, and copying continues to 1372
The Kan'ei Kojiki, the first printed edition, is published in Kyoto
Motoori Norinaga completes the Kojiki-den, his 44-volume study begun in 1764
Basil Hall Chamberlain publishes his English translation of the Kojiki
Tsuda Sōkichi argues that the Kojiki is a document created to legitimise the rule of the imperial line

sections.origins:
It is believed that the compilation of genealogical and anecdotal histories of the imperial Yamato court and of prominent clans began under Emperors Keitai and Kinmei in the 6th century. The first concerted effort at historical compilation of which a record survives was made in 620 under Prince Shotoku and Soga no Umako. According to the Nihon Shoki, it produced the Tennōki, or Record of the Emperors, the Kokki, or National Record, and other fundamental records concerning influential clans. Only the Kokki survived the burning of Soga no Emishi's estate, where the documents were kept, during the Isshi incident of 645, and it was apparently lost soon after.

The preface of the Kojiki says that leading families also kept their own historical and genealogical records, and gives the correction of errors that had supposedly crept into them as one reason for the work. It says that Emperor Tenmu, who reigned from 673 to 686, ordered the clan documents reviewed and commissioned a court attendant of exceptional memory, Hieda no Are, to memorise the records and oral traditions of the imperial lineage. Nothing further happened until the reign of Empress Genmei, who reigned from 707 to 715.
sections.content:
The Kojiki recounts the mythological creation of Japan, the genealogy of the Japanese gods, the kami, and the histories of the semi-legendary early emperors. It has three parts. The Kamitsumaki, or upper volume, holds the preface and the Age of the Gods: the pair Izanagi and Izanami shape the islands, Izanami dies and Izanagi flees the land of the dead, Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo are born from his washing, and Amaterasu hides in a rock cave until the gods lure her out. Susanoo slays the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi, Ōkuninushi rules the earthly land until the heavenly deities pacify it, and Ninigi, Amaterasu's grandson, descends to Kyūshū as the progenitor of the imperial line.

The Nakatsumaki, or middle volume, begins with Jimmu's conquests, which make him the first emperor, and ends with the 15th emperor, Ōjin. The reigns of the second to ninth emperors are given in a minimum of detail, with only names, descendants and the locations of palaces and tombs. The Shimotsumaki, or lower volume, covers the 16th to 33rd emperors and has far fewer dealings with deities. Its narrative also holds dozens of short songs and poems, often spoken by gods, heroes or early rulers.
sections.making:
According to the preface, Empress Genmei ordered the courtier Ō no Yasumaro on the 18th of the 9th month of 711 to record what Hieda no Are had learned. Yasumaro wrote the information down in Classical Chinese and presented his work to the empress on the 28th of the 1st month of 712. The preface is a dedicatory address to Genmei that opens with a poem summarising the work, and it ends with a brief explanation of the Chinese characters used to transcribe native Japanese words and of the division into three volumes.

The book is written mostly in Classical Chinese, but the songs are in Old Japanese, written in man'yōgana, a system in which Chinese characters represent the syllables of Old Japanese purely phonetically. The Kojiki is a collation of different traditions woven into a single official mythology, made to justify the rule of the Yamato polity and to give different interest groups a place in the national genealogy. Other possible factors were interest in the nation's origins after the influx of foreign culture and the need for an authoritative genealogy by which to judge the claims of noble families and reorganise them into a new system of ranks and titles. Unlike the Nihon Shoki of 720, which drew on varied sources including Chinese texts, the Kojiki is apparently based on sources handed down within the court.
sections.reception:
Because the Nihon Shoki was one of the six imperial histories, it was widely read and studied in the Heian period, while the Kojiki was mostly treated as an ancillary text. A work known as the Sendai Kuji Hongi, claimed to be by Prince Shōtoku and Soga no Umako, was considered earlier and more reliable; modern scholarly consensus holds it to be a Heian period forgery based on the Kojiki and the Shoki. By the Kamakura period few people had access to the Kojiki, particularly to its middle volume.

The Edo period's nativist scholars, the kokugaku, saw Japan's earliest writings as the repository of a uniquely superior Japanese identity, and the Kojiki gained the status of a sacred text. Kada no Azumamaro and Kamo no Mabuchi produced annotated versions. Motoori Norinaga, who met Mabuchi in 1763, regarded it as a true account of actual events that, read correctly, could reveal Japan as a community where the kami, the emperor and the people lived in harmony. Under State Shintō, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki achieved a scriptural status and their stories were treated as orthodox national history. Scholars who questioned their veracity faced censorship, forced resignation or even trial.
sections.survival:
The Kojiki is available only in comparatively late manuscripts, owing to the neglect it suffered by the Kamakura period. There are two major branches, the Ise and the Urabe. The extant Urabe branch consists of 36 manuscripts, all based on the 1522 copies by Urabe Kanenaga. The Ise branch divides into the Shinpukuji-bon manuscript of 1371–1372 and the Dōka-bon manuscripts: the Dōka-bon of 1381, of which only the first half of the first volume remains, the Dōshō-bon of 1424, of which only the first volume remains with many defects, and the Shun'yu-bon of 1426.

The Shinpukuji-bon is the oldest existing manuscript. Although it is classed in the Ise branch, it is a mixture of the two. The monk Ken'yu based his copy on that of Ōnakatomi Sadayo, who in 1266 copied volumes one and three but could not obtain the second. In 1282 he gained access to the second volume through an Urabe-branch manuscript and transcribed it. With printing, the Kojiki first reached a wide audience: the Kan'ei Kojiki was published in Kyoto in 1644, and a second edition, the Gōtō Kojiki, was printed in 1687 by Deguchi Nobuyoshi, a priest at Ise Shrine.
sections.legacy:
The myths of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki are part of the inspiration behind many practices and the unified Shinto orthodoxy, and they were later incorporated into practices such as the misogi purification ritual. The text also finalised, and possibly formulated, the framework by which Japanese history was examined in terms of the reigns of emperors.

In the Meiji period the introduction of philology and comparative mythology brought renewed scholarly attention, and scholars recognised the Kojiki's literary value and noted that its accounts resembled ancient Greek and Roman myths. In 1913 Tsuda Sōkichi argued that, particularly in its earlier sections, it was neither history nor myth but a document created to legitimise the imperial line. His conclusions caused controversy, and later scholarship, particularly after World War II, largely develops and corrects his line of thought. Watsuji Tetsurō argued in 1920 for a literary appreciation, and Kurano Kenji proposed in 1927 that it be compared with Western epic literature and regarded as a national epic like Beowulf. Editions, translations and commentaries have continued to appear, among the English translations those of Chamberlain in 1882, Philippi in 1968 and 1969, and Heldt in 2014.

summary: The Kojiki is an early Japanese chronicle of myths, genealogies and songs, which its preface says Ō no Yasumaro wrote down for Empress Genmei in 711–712. It presents the Yamato line as descended from the gods, was neglected for centuries, and was elevated by Edo nativists.
references: John S. Brownlee, Political Thought in Japanese Historical Writing: From Kojiki (712) to Tokushi Yoron (1712) (Wilfrid Laurier University Press, 1991)
John S. Brownlee, Japanese Historians and the National Myths, 1600–1945: The Age of the Gods and Emperor Jimmu (University of British Columbia Press, 1997)
Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press and University of Tokyo Press, 1968)
Gustav Heldt, The Kojiki: An Account of Ancient Matters (Columbia University Press, 2014)
notes: The article says Hoori reigned 580 years at Takachiho; left out as a mythic figure.
The synopsis of the Nakatsumaki and Shimotsumaki is only a list of headings in the article; their contents are described from the Structure section.
Event 1882 is the date of Chamberlain's translation; the article lists it first among English translations but does not say it was the first, so the event says only that he published his translation.

Start 711 is the preface's date of the order to Yasumaro; the work was presented in 712. The article says the preface 'claims' composition by Yasumaro, hedged in the text as 'according to the preface'.
The earliest manuscript statement 'neglect' as cause is the article's own wording ('due to this neglect').
